title: Customer value-based pricing strategies: why companies resist
author_source: Hinterhuber, A., Journal of Business Strategy 29(4), 41-50, 2008, article
note: Short, readable diagnosis of why firms default to cost-plus or competition-based pricing although value-based pricing performs better. Names five obstacles (value assessment, value communication, market segmentation, sales force management, senior management support) and gives remedies. Includes survey evidence on how common each of the three orientations is.
course_use: Core opening reading for the session on pricing orientations; use the five obstacles as a discussion grid for student companies. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Emerald).

title: Industrial product pricing: a value-based approach
author_source: Liozu, S. M.; Hinterhuber, A., Journal of Business Strategy 33(4), 28-39, 2012, article
note: Case-based account of industrial (B2B) firms moving from cost-plus to value-based pricing. Describes the roles of champions, pricing teams and value quantification tools during the transition.
course_use: Companion to Hinterhuber 2008 for B2B-oriented MBA groups; good for a 'how to implement' discussion. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Mindful pricing: transforming organizations through value-based pricing
author_source: Liozu, S. M.; Hinterhuber, A.; Perelli, S.; Boland, R., Journal of Strategic Marketing 20(3), 197-209, 2012, article
note: Grounded-theory study of firms adopting value-based pricing. Frames the change as an organizational transformation that needs CEO championing, confidence building and cross-functional capabilities, not just a switch of technique.
course_use: Background reading for the change-management side of pricing; pairs well with a guest speaker from industry. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Taylor & Francis).

title: Pricing orientation, pricing capabilities, and firm performance
author_source: Liozu, S. M.; Hinterhuber, A., Management Decision 51(3), 594-614, 2013, article
note: Survey of industrial firms linking value-based pricing orientation and pricing capabilities to firm performance. Value-based orientation is positively related to performance; cost-based orientation is not. Gives a usable operationalisation of the three orientations.
course_use: Evidence slide for 'does value-based pricing pay off?'; discuss the limits of survey and self-report data. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Best Practices for New Product Pricing: Impact on Market Performance and Price Level under Different Conditions
author_source: Ingenbleek, P. T. M.; Frambach, R. T.; Verhallen, T. M. M., Journal of Product Innovation Management 30(3), 560-573, 2013, article
note: Survey of new product launches: value-informed pricing improves market performance, while cost- and competition-informed practices matter under specific conditions (e.g., competitive intensity, product advantage). Nuances the 'value is always best' message.
course_use: Reading for new product pricing; use the contingency results to challenge simplistic value-based dogma. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Wiley).

title: Successful New Product Pricing Practices: A Contingency Approach
author_source: Ingenbleek, P.; Debruyne, M.; Frambach, R. T.; Verhallen, T. M. M., Marketing Letters 14(4), 289-305, 2003, article
note: Classic empirical paper: use of customer value information is the strongest driver of new product success; cost and competitor information add to it depending on market conditions.
course_use: Short classic; background reading, or assign to students who want the original contingency framework. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Springer).

title: Value quantification capabilities in industrial markets
author_source: Hinterhuber, A., Journal of Business Research 76, 163-178, 2017, article
note: Qualitative study of how B2B suppliers quantify and document customer value (value calculators, case studies, TCO tools) and why this capability drives value-based selling and pricing. Offers a typology of value quantification approaches.
course_use: B2B pricing session; students build a simple value calculator for a case product. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Elsevier).

title: Organizational and institutional barriers to value-based pricing in industrial relationships
author_source: Töytäri, P.; Rajala, R.; Alejandro, T. B., Industrial Marketing Management 47, 53-64, 2015, article
note: Identifies barriers on both the supplier and the buyer side (procurement practices, risk aversion, lack of trust, institutional norms) that block value-based pricing in B2B relationships. Useful because it adds the buyer perspective that Hinterhuber leaves out.
course_use: Discussion: why procurement departments resist value-based prices; supplier vs. buyer role-play. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Is innovation in pricing your next source of competitive advantage?
author_source: Hinterhuber, A.; Liozu, S. M., Business Horizons 57(3), 413-423, 2014, article
note: Practitioner-oriented framework of pricing innovation (pricing strategy, price setting, pricing models such as pay-per-use, outcome-based or freemium) with many company examples. An accessible bridge to new revenue models.
course_use: Easy MBA reading to introduce innovative pricing models before the freemium, subscription and AI sessions. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Elsevier).

title: Is It Time to Rethink Your Pricing Strategy?
author_source: Hinterhuber, A.; Liozu, S. M., MIT Sloan Management Review 53(4), 69-77, 2012, article
note: Managerial article arguing that pricing is an underused strategic lever. Contrasts cost-, competition- and value-based approaches and outlines steps to build pricing as an organizational capability. Volume and pages from memory; the URL returned 403 to an automated check, so verify both.
course_use: Pre-class reading for executive/MBA groups; quick and good for discussion. Paid (MIT SMR), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Pricing process as a capability: a resource-based perspective
author_source: Dutta, S.; Zbaracki, M. J.; Bergen, M., Strategic Management Journal 24(7), 615-630, 2003, article
note: Seminal argument, based on an in-depth case of a large manufacturer, that the pricing process itself (setting prices and convincing customers and internal stakeholders) is a hard-to-imitate capability and a source of competitive advantage.
course_use: Theory anchor for the pricing capabilities block; connects to the resource-based view from strategy courses. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Wiley).

title: Managerial and Customer Costs of Price Adjustment: Direct Evidence from Industrial Markets
author_source: Zbaracki, M. J.; Ritson, M.; Levy, D.; Dutta, S.; Bergen, M., Review of Economics and Statistics 86(2), 514-533, 2004, article
note: Measures the real costs of changing prices in a large industrial firm. Managerial costs (information gathering, decision making) and customer costs (negotiation, communication) far exceed physical menu costs. Strong data on why price increases are hard, which makes it relevant to inflation-era pricing.
course_use: Use in the inflation and price-increase session; the cost figures make a strong slide. WU-Lizenz prüfen (MIT Press).

title: How to Organize Pricing? Vertical Delegation and Horizontal Dispersion of Pricing Authority
author_source: Homburg, C.; Jensen, O.; Hahn, A., Journal of Marketing 76(5), 49-69, 2012, article
note: German multi-industry study (Mannheim) on who should hold pricing authority. Delegating pricing to sales and spreading it across functions affect pricing performance, depending on market conditions. Rare evidence on how to organize the pricing function.
course_use: Discussion on delegating price authority to the sales force in B2B; German research example. WU-Lizenz prüfen (SAGE/AMA).

title: Versioning: The Smart Way to Sell Information
author_source: Shapiro, C.; Varian, H. R., Harvard Business Review 76(6), 1998, article
note: Classic managerial piece on second-degree price discrimination for information goods: create versions that differ in speed, convenience, features or support so customers sort themselves. Includes the 'Goldilocks' three-version logic.
course_use: Reading for price customization; students design good-better-best tiers for a digital product (e.g., an AI assistant). Paid HBR, usually available via EBSCO, WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Strategic Bundling of Products and Prices: A New Synthesis for Marketing
author_source: Stremersch, S.; Tellis, G. J., Journal of Marketing 66(1), 55-72, 2002, article
note: Standard taxonomy separating price bundling from product bundling, and pure from mixed bundling, with legal and strategic implications. Clears up terms students routinely confuse.
course_use: Required reading for the bundling session; students use the framework to classify real offers (telecom, streaming bundles). WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: A Probabilistic Approach to Pricing a Bundle of Products or Services
author_source: Venkatesh, R.; Mahajan, V., Journal of Marketing Research 30(4), 494-508, 1993, article
note: Model of optimal pure vs. mixed bundling based on reservation price distributions, applied to entertainment services; shows when mixed bundling dominates. Technical, but the intuition is teachable.
course_use: Background for quantitatively inclined groups; can be paired with a spreadsheet exercise on reservation prices. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Making "Freemium" Work
author_source: Kumar, V., Harvard Business Review 92(5), 27-29, 2014, article
note: Short practitioner guide to designing freemium: what to give away, how to limit the free tier and how to convert users. Examples include Dropbox and Skype. An accessible starting point.
course_use: Pre-reading before Gu et al. (2018); students audit the free/premium split of a freemium app. Paid HBR, WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Selling the Premium in Freemium
author_source: Gu, X.; Kannan, P. K.; Ma, L., Journal of Marketing 82(6), 10-27, 2018, article
note: Empirical study of a freemium service showing how the free version and the feature and capacity gap to premium drive upgrades. The free tier can both cannibalize and stimulate premium demand. Gives managers concrete levers for tier design.
course_use: Core academic reading for freemium; discussion on the optimal gap between tiers. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Paying Too Much and Being Happy about It: Existence, Causes, and Consequences of Tariff-Choice Biases
author_source: Lambrecht, A.; Skiera, B., Journal of Marketing Research 43(2), 212-223, 2006, article
note: German study (Skiera, Frankfurt) using internet-access billing data. Many customers choose flat rates even when pay-per-use would be cheaper (flat-rate bias), driven by insurance, taxi-meter and convenience effects. Flat-rate bias does not raise churn; pay-per-use bias does.
course_use: Key reading for subscription vs. usage-based pricing; ask students why SaaS and LLM providers offer flat plans. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Does Uncertainty Matter? Consumer Behavior Under Three-Part Tariffs
author_source: Lambrecht, A.; Seim, K.; Skiera, B., Marketing Science 26(5), 698-710, 2007, article
note: Models plan choice and usage under three-part tariffs (fee, allowance, overage price) and shows that usage uncertainty is central to plan choice and revenue. Conceptual basis for the allowance and credit-based plans used by SaaS and AI tools.
course_use: Background for usage-based and credit-based SaaS/AI pricing; technical, so assign to selected students. WU-Lizenz prüfen (INFORMS).

title: When Talk Is "Free": The Effect of Tariff Structure on Usage under Two- and Three-Part Tariffs
author_source: Ascarza, E.; Lambrecht, A.; Vilcassim, N., Journal of Marketing Research 49(6), 882-899, 2012, article
note: Telecom field data showing that the tariff structure itself changes usage beyond pure price effects: a 'free' allowance under three-part tariffs boosts consumption. Relevant for designing tiers with included usage.
course_use: Discussion: how included credits in AI/SaaS plans change customer behaviour. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Planning New Tariffs at tele.ring: The Application and Impact of an Integrated Segmentation, Targeting, and Positioning Tool
author_source: Natter, M.; Mild, A.; Wagner, U.; Taudes, A., Marketing Science 27(4), 600-609, 2008, article
note: WU Vienna Practice Prize report on how the Austrian mobile operator tele.ring used a segmentation and choice-based decision-support tool to design new tariffs, with documented profit impact. A local example proven in practice. German-language version: Marketing ZFP 29(3), 2007.
course_use: Excellent Austrian case input for tariff design; possible link to a guest lecture by WU faculty. WU-Lizenz prüfen (INFORMS).

title: Product Selling vs. Pay-Per-Use Service: A Strategic Analysis of Competing Business Models
author_source: Ladas, K.; Kavadias, S.; Loch, C., Management Science, 2021/2022, article
note: Analytical model of when pay-per-use (product-as-a-service) beats selling: low delivery costs and uncertainty about customer usage favour pay-per-use, especially at mid-range production costs. Volume and issue not checked.
course_use: Background for servitization and usage-based B2B models (e.g., Hilti fleet management, Rolls-Royce 'power by the hour'). WU-Lizenz prüfen (INFORMS).

title: Pay today, or delay the pay: Consumer preference for double flat-rate pricing plans
author_source: Schuster, E.; et al., Journal of Business Research, article 114804, 2024, article
note: Choice experiments on plans that combine a one-off fee with a recurring subscription, common for connected-car and digital add-on services. Consumers prefer single flat rates and weigh one-off fees more heavily than recurring fees.
course_use: Recent evidence for subscription design in automotive/IoT; discuss BMW-style feature subscriptions. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Pricing and the Psychology of Consumption
author_source: Gourville, J.; Soman, D., Harvard Business Review 80(9), 90-96, 2002, article
note: Shows that the timing and bundling of payments affects usage: payment depreciation (e.g., annual vs. monthly gym fees) reduces consumption and future renewals. Directly relevant to subscription design and churn.
course_use: Use in the subscription session; ask how annual vs. monthly SaaS billing affects churn. Paid HBR, WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Menu Pricing of Large Language Models
author_source: Bergemann, D.; Bonatti, A.; Smolin, A., arXiv preprint 2502.07736, 2025, article (working paper)
note: Economic theory of how LLM providers should design menus of token budgets. Explains committed-spend contracts, minimum and maximum spend plans, multi-model versioning and the linear API pricing seen at Anthropic, OpenAI and GitHub. Working paper, not yet peer reviewed.
course_use: Frontier reading for the AI pricing session; non-technical students read the introduction and the section that maps the theory to observed price lists. Open access (arXiv).

title: How to Use Generative AI for Pricing
author_source: Cohen, M. C., MIT Sloan Management Review, 2026, article
note: Practitioner article on using LLMs (through prompts rather than custom code) to support retail pricing decisions, with implementation examples and caveats on consistency, explainability and bias. The DOI comes from the search index and was not resolved.
course_use: Pair with a class exercise: students prompt an LLM for a price recommendation and critique it. Paid (MIT SMR), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Algorithmic Collusion by Large Language Models
author_source: Fish, S.; Gonczarowski, Y. A.; Shorrer, R. I., arXiv preprint 2404.00806, 2024, article (working paper)
note: Experiments in which LLM-based pricing agents in oligopoly settings reach supracompetitive prices on their own; small changes in prompt wording change how much they collude. A strong illustration of the risks of delegating pricing to AI agents. Preprint.
course_use: Discussion on AI agents setting prices and competition law; link to Calvano et al. (2020). Open access.

title: Do All Languages Cost the Same? Tokenization in the Era of Commercial Language Models
author_source: Ahia, O.; et al., arXiv 2305.13707 (EMNLP 2023), 2023, article
note: Shows that per-token API pricing charges speakers of many languages more for the same content, because the same text needs more tokens, and often gives them worse quality. A concrete fairness problem with usage-based AI pricing metrics.
course_use: Short discussion case on choosing a pricing metric (tokens vs. tasks vs. outcomes) and its fairness; relevant to German-speaking users too. Open access.

title: Dynamic pricing and learning: Historical origins, current research, and new directions
author_source: den Boer, A. V., Surveys in Operations Research and Management Science 20(1), 1-18, 2015, article
note: Standard review of dynamic pricing with demand learning (explore vs. exploit), from early economics to modern revenue management algorithms. Gives students the vocabulary behind 'algorithmic pricing'.
course_use: Background reading for instructors and quantitatively interested students. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Elsevier).

title: An Empirical Analysis of Algorithmic Pricing on Amazon Marketplace
author_source: Chen, L.; Mislove, A.; Wilson, C., Proceedings of the 25th International Conference on World Wide Web (WWW), 1339-1349, 2016, article
note: Detects roughly 500 Amazon sellers using algorithmic pricing, often matching or pegging to competitors. These sellers win the Buy Box more often and change prices far more frequently. An accessible empirical picture of repricing bots.
course_use: Case-style reading; students check a product's price history (e.g., with Keepa) and discuss. Free (WWW proceedings are openly available).

title: Artificial Intelligence, Algorithmic Pricing, and Collusion
author_source: Calvano, E.; Calzolari, G.; Denicolò, V.; Pastorello, S., American Economic Review 110(10), 3267-3297, 2020, article
note: Simulations showing that Q-learning pricing algorithms learn to sustain supracompetitive prices with punishment strategies, without communicating. Key reference in the competition-policy debate on AI pricing.
course_use: Read the introduction and conclusions only; discussion on regulating pricing algorithms. WU-Lizenz prüfen (AEA).

title: An Assortmentwide Decision-Support System for Dynamic Pricing and Promotion Planning in DIY Retailing
author_source: Natter, M.; Reutterer, T.; Mild, A.; Taudes, A., Marketing Science 26(4), 576-583, 2007, article
note: WU Vienna Practice Prize report on the pricing and promotion decision-support system implemented at the Austrian DIY retailer bauMax. Documents demand modelling across the assortment and the resulting profit gains.
course_use: Austrian real-world case of data-driven retail pricing; ideal as a WU-specific example or guest talk. WU-Lizenz prüfen (INFORMS).

title: Skimming or Penetration? Strategic Dynamic Pricing for New Products
author_source: Spann, M.; Fischer, M.; Tellis, G. J., Marketing Science 34(2), 235-249, 2015, article
note: Analysis of launch price paths for thousands of consumer electronics products, including digital cameras. Skimming dominates, but penetration and stable prices occur depending on brand and market conditions. A data-based answer to the textbook skimming vs. penetration question (Spann, LMU Munich).
course_use: New product pricing session; students predict the price path of a new gadget. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Using Big Data to Estimate Consumer Surplus: The Case of Uber
author_source: Cohen, P.; Hahn, R.; Hall, J.; Levitt, S.; Metcalfe, R., NBER Working Paper 22627, 2016, article (working paper)
note: Uses the discontinuities in Uber's surge multiplier to estimate demand curves. Finds that UberX generated about 6.8 billion USD of US consumer surplus in 2015, roughly 1.60 USD per dollar spent. Shows how dynamic prices reveal willingness to pay.
course_use: Excellent bridge between pricing strategy and WTP; discuss the regression discontinuity logic. NBER working paper, free download (some networks require login).

title: The Role of Surge Pricing on a Service Platform with Self-Scheduling Capacity
author_source: Cachon, G. P.; Daniels, K. M.; Lobel, R., Manufacturing & Service Operations Management 19(3), 368-384, 2017, article
note: Model showing that surge pricing, though not fully optimal, earns near-optimal profit and can benefit platforms, drivers and riders, because it matches self-scheduling supply to peak demand. A counterweight to popular criticism. Volume and pages from memory.
course_use: Debate format, 'surge pricing is fair': this paper for the pro side, Xu et al. (2024) and the fairness papers for the con side. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Customer Voice on Two-Sided Platforms: The Effect of Surge Pricing on Customer Complaints
author_source: Xu, L.; et al., Management Science, 2024, article
note: Ride-sharing data: surge makes a driver about 1.13 times more likely to receive a complaint, and surge-induced complaints offset about 23% of the driver's surge gain. Capping surge reduced complaints and increased platform usage. Shows hidden costs of dynamic pricing.
course_use: Recent evidence for the dynamic pricing fairness discussion. WU-Lizenz prüfen (INFORMS).

title: Matching and Pricing in Ride Hailing: Wild Goose Chases and How to Solve Them
author_source: Castillo, J. C.; Knoepfle, D.; Weyl, E. G., Management Science, 2024, article
note: Explains why surge pricing exists: without it, high demand causes 'wild goose chases' (drivers sent on long pickups) and efficiency collapses. Surge pricing works better than fixes to the matching algorithm. Gives the economic rationale students often miss.
course_use: Background for instructors; summarise the mechanism on one slide. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: The Price Is Unfair! A Conceptual Framework of Price Fairness Perceptions
author_source: Xia, L.; Monroe, K. B.; Cox, J. L., Journal of Marketing 68(4), 1-15, 2004, article
note: Standard conceptual framework. Fairness judgments come from comparisons with other transactions, are shaped by perceived seller motives, trust and the buyer-seller relationship, and lead to emotions and behaviours such as complaints and switching.
course_use: Core reading for the fairness block; framework for analysing personalized pricing, surge and shrinkflation cases. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Consumer Perceptions of Price (Un)Fairness
author_source: Bolton, L. E.; Warlop, L.; Alba, J. W., Journal of Consumer Research 29(4), 474-491, 2003, article
note: Experiments showing that consumers overestimate retailer profits and underestimate costs, and judge prices unfair partly because they ignore many cost components. Fairness judgments improve when costs are explained.
course_use: Discussion on communicating price increases through cost transparency; use in the inflation session. WU-Lizenz prüfen (OUP).

title: Fairness as a Constraint on Profit Seeking: Entitlements in the Market
author_source: Kahneman, D.; Knetsch, J. L.; Thaler, R. H., American Economic Review 76(4), 728-741, 1986, article
note: Origin of the dual-entitlement principle: price increases justified by cost increases are seen as fair, while those that exploit demand shifts (the snow shovel after a storm) are seen as unfair. The survey vignettes are ideal for in-class replication. JSTOR stable URL not checked.
course_use: In-class vote replicating the snow-shovel scenario before discussing surge pricing. WU-Lizenz prüfen (JSTOR).

title: Customers' Reactions to Price Increases: Do Customer Satisfaction and Perceived Motive Fairness Matter?
author_source: Homburg, C.; Hoyer, W. D.; Koschate, N., Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 33(1), 36-49, 2005, article
note: German experimental study: satisfied customers react less negatively to price increases, but only if they see the seller's motive as fair. Perceived motive fairness is the key lever. Directly applicable to the 2022-2024 inflation price increases.
course_use: Reading for 'how to raise prices'; students draft a price-increase letter applying the findings. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Springer).

title: How price increases affect future purchases: The role of mental budgeting, income, and framing
author_source: Homburg, C.; Koschate, N.; Totzek, D., Psychology & Marketing 27(1), 36-53, 2010, article
note: Shows that price increases reduce future purchases through mental budgeting, moderated by income and by how the increase is framed. Complements Homburg et al. (2005) with downstream behavioural effects.
course_use: Optional reading for the inflation and price-increase session. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Wiley).

title: Dynamic Pricing and Consumer Fairness Perceptions
author_source: Haws, K. L.; Bearden, W. O., Journal of Consumer Research 33(3), 304-311, 2006, article
note: Experiments comparing price differences across consumers, across time and across sellers. Differences between consumers (same seller, same time) are judged most unfair, and prices set by the seller are judged more harshly than auction-set prices.
course_use: Short reading; good basis for discussing online personalized prices and the Amazon DVD controversy. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Personalized Pricing and Consumer Welfare
author_source: Dubé, J.-P.; Misra, S., Journal of Political Economy 131(1), 2023, article
note: Field experiment at ZipRecruiter with machine-learning personalized prices. Personalization raises profit by a further 19% over the optimized uniform price; total consumer surplus falls, but more than 60% of consumers benefit. Rare large-scale real-world evidence. Volume and issue from memory.
course_use: Key reading for personalized pricing; debate whether firms should personalize. Read the introduction and results. WU-Lizenz prüfen (UChicago Press).

title: Seeking the perfect price: Consumer responses to personalized price discrimination in e-commerce
author_source: Hufnagel, G.; et al., Journal of Business Research, 2022, article
note: Three online experiments: personalized pricing triggers negative attitudes and behaviour, mediated by fairness perceptions, among disadvantaged and even price-favoured customers, whatever personal data are used.
course_use: Recent evidence for the personalized pricing debate; contrast with Dubé and Misra's welfare view. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: A special price just for you: effects of personalized dynamic pricing on consumer fairness perceptions
author_source: Priester, A.; Robbert, T.; Roth, S., Journal of Revenue and Pricing Management 19, 2020, article
note: German experiments: individual prices are seen as less fair than segment prices, and location-based pricing as less fair than pricing based on purchase history. Privacy concerns moderate these effects.
course_use: Short, practical reading for designing acceptable price differentiation. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Springer/Palgrave).

title: Demographic Pricing in the Digital Age: Assessing Fairness Perceptions in Algorithmic versus Human-Based Price Discrimination
author_source: Duani, N.; Barasch, A.; Morwitz, V., Journal of the Association for Consumer Research, 2024, article
note: Consumers see demographic price discrimination as fairer when an algorithm rather than a human sets the price, because they feel less judged. The effect weakens for time-based discrimination and when the discrimination serves a prosocial goal. Counterintuitive and good for discussion.
course_use: Discussion starter: should firms disclose that 'an algorithm' sets the price? WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: New developments in behavioral pricing research
author_source: Koschate-Fischer, N.; Wüllner, K., Journal of Business Economics 87(6), 809-875, 2017, article
note: Comprehensive review by German authors (Erlangen-Nürnberg) structuring behavioural pricing research: price information processing, price perceptions (reference prices, price endings, partitioning), fairness and WTP, with a research agenda.
course_use: Ideal one-stop background reading for the behavioural pricing block; assign sections. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Springer).

title: Effects of $9 Price Endings on Retail Sales: Evidence from Field Experiments
author_source: Anderson, E. T.; Simester, D., Quantitative Marketing and Economics 1(1), 93-110, 2003, article
note: Mail-order catalogue field experiments: 9-ending prices increased demand, even compared with lower prices, with stronger effects for new items. Suggests that 9-endings signal a good deal.
course_use: Classic field-experiment example; students design their own A/B test of price endings. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Springer).

title: Penny Wise and Pound Foolish: The Left-Digit Effect in Price Cognition
author_source: Thomas, M.; Morwitz, V., Journal of Consumer Research 32(1), 54-64, 2005, article
note: Shows that 9-ending prices are perceived as clearly lower only when the leftmost digit changes (2.99 vs. 3.00, but not 3.59 vs. 3.60). Explains the mechanism: anchoring on the left digit while encoding the price.
course_use: Pair with Anderson and Simester; quick in-class demo. WU-Lizenz prüfen (OUP).

title: The price-perceived quality relationship: A meta-analytic review and assessment of its determinants
author_source: Völckner, F.; Hofmann, J., Marketing Letters 18(3), 181-196, 2007, article
note: Meta-analysis by German authors of studies on inferring quality from price. The price-quality effect has weakened over time and depends on product category, the information available and study design.
course_use: Evidence for when high prices signal quality (discussion of premium and luxury positioning). WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Reference Price Research: Review and Propositions
author_source: Mazumdar, T.; Raj, S. P.; Sinha, I., Journal of Marketing 69(4), 84-102, 2005, article
note: Standard review of internal and external reference prices: how they form, how they are measured, how they affect choice, and what managers should do (e.g., 'was/now' prices, promotion frequency).
course_use: Core reading for reference price effects; use with strikethrough-price examples from Austrian retailers. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Divide and Prosper: Consumers' Reactions to Partitioned Prices
author_source: Morwitz, V. G.; Greenleaf, E. A.; Johnson, E. J., Journal of Marketing Research 35(4), 453-463, 1998, article
note: Classic experiments: splitting a price into a base price plus a surcharge (e.g., shipping) lowers the recalled total cost and raises demand compared with all-in prices.
course_use: Use with the drip pricing papers to discuss where partitioning becomes deceptive. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: The price does not include additional taxes, fees, and surcharges: A review of research on partitioned pricing
author_source: Greenleaf, E. A.; Johnson, E. J.; Morwitz, V. G.; Shalev, E., Journal of Consumer Psychology 26(1), 105-124, 2016, article
note: Review of more than 15 years of partitioned pricing research. Explains when partitioning helps (small, benefit-related surcharges) and when it hurts (surcharges seen as unfair), and covers related tactics such as drip pricing.
course_use: Background review for the price presentation block. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Wiley).

title: Consumer Reactions to Drip Pricing
author_source: Santana, S.; Dallas, S. K.; Morwitz, V. G., Marketing Science 39(1), 188-210, 2020, article
note: Experiments showing that drip pricing (fees revealed late in the purchase process) makes consumers more likely to end up with a more expensive option and less likely to keep searching, but raises dissatisfaction once they discover the fees.
course_use: Core reading for drip pricing; link to EU/US 'junk fee' regulation and ticketing examples. WU-Lizenz prüfen (INFORMS).

title: Price Salience and Product Choice
author_source: Blake, T.; Moshary, S.; Sweeney, K.; Tadelis, S., Marketing Science 40(4), 619-636, 2021, article
note: Large natural field experiment at StubHub: showing fees only at checkout raised revenue and led buyers to choose more expensive tickets than upfront all-in pricing did. Hard data on the effect of drip pricing.
course_use: Pair with Santana et al.; ask whether short-term gains justify the practice. WU-Lizenz prüfen; NBER working paper version (w25186) free.

title: Many a little makes a mickle: Why do consumers negatively react to sequential price disclosure?
author_source: Totzek, D.; et al., Psychology & Marketing 37, 2020, article
note: Eye-tracking study (n = 225): disclosing the final price step by step rather than upfront lowers perceived fairness. It works through more attention to the final price, higher perceived price complexity and lower perceived transparency, especially when there are many surcharges.
course_use: Recent German evidence on how drip pricing works. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Wiley).

title: Why Regulate Junk Fees?
author_source: Mahoney, N., Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2025, article
note: Accessible essay on hidden mandatory fees (tickets, hotels, cable, restaurants, banking). Explains how they raise search costs and prices and why disclosure and competition are often not enough, and reviews recent all-in pricing rules.
course_use: Policy reading for the drip pricing and fairness session. Free (JEP is open access).

title: How price complexity takes its toll: The neglected role of a simplicity bias and fairness in price evaluations
author_source: Homburg, C.; Totzek, D.; Krämer, M., Journal of Business Research 67(6), 1114-1122, 2014, article
note: German experiments showing that complex price structures are perceived as less fair and less attractive (a simplicity bias), even when they are objectively cheaper.
course_use: Useful for tariff and SaaS plan design; students simplify a complex price list. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Adding Asymmetrically Dominated Alternatives: Violations of Regularity and the Similarity Hypothesis
author_source: Huber, J.; Payne, J. W.; Puto, C., Journal of Consumer Research 9(1), 90-98, 1982, article
note: Original demonstration of the decoy (attraction) effect: adding an inferior option increases the choice share of the option that dominates it. Basis for decoy tiers in price menus, such as the well-known Economist subscription example.
course_use: Classic for the price menu and decoy session; run a live poll replication. WU-Lizenz prüfen (OUP).

title: Choice Based on Reasons: The Case of Attraction and Compromise Effects
author_source: Simonson, I., Journal of Consumer Research 16(2), 158-174, 1989, article
note: Shows that consumers prefer middle options (compromise effect) and dominating options (attraction effect) because these choices are easier to justify. Explains why good-better-best menus steer choice to the middle tier.
course_use: Pair with Huber et al. (1982) and with versioning (Shapiro and Varian). WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Pay What You Want: A New Participative Pricing Mechanism
author_source: Kim, J.-Y.; Natter, M.; Spann, M., Journal of Marketing 73(1), 44-58, 2009, article
note: Field studies (restaurant, cinema, delicatessen) co-authored by Natter and Spann. Pay-what-you-want prices are mostly above zero, driven by fairness, satisfaction and price consciousness, and the mechanism can be profitable in some settings.
course_use: Engaging discussion case on participative pricing (e.g., Radiohead, museums); German-speaking authors. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Pricing to Create Shared Value
author_source: Bertini, M.; Gourville, J. T., Harvard Business Review 90(6), 2012, article
note: Argues that pricing should share value with customers rather than only extract it. Principles include giving customers choice and control, pricing on the value delivered, and being fair and transparent, with examples from airlines, software and music.
course_use: Discussion reading linking fairness and strategy; a good closing piece. Paid HBR, WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: The Long-Term Impact of Promotion and Advertising on Consumer Brand Choice
author_source: Mela, C. F.; Gupta, S.; Lehmann, D. R., Journal of Marketing Research 34(2), 248-261, 1997, article
note: Eight years of panel data: frequent price promotions make consumers more price- and promotion-sensitive over time, while advertising reduces price sensitivity. Core evidence on the long-term costs of promotions.
course_use: Reading for the price promotion session; debate whether promotions work 'like a drug'. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: The Long-Term Effects of Price Promotions on Category Incidence, Brand Choice, and Purchase Quantity
author_source: Pauwels, K.; Hanssens, D. M.; Siddarth, S., Journal of Marketing Research 39(4), 421-439, 2002, article
note: Persistence modelling shows that promotion effects on category incidence, brand choice and quantity mostly die out within weeks; permanent effects are rare. Nuances the Mela et al. findings.
course_use: Pair with Mela et al. (1997) for a balanced view. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Do Promotions Benefit Manufacturers, Retailers, or Both?
author_source: Srinivasan, S.; Pauwels, K.; Hanssens, D. M.; Dekimpe, M. G., Management Science 50(5), 617-629, 2004, article
note: Analysis of 25 categories: price promotions usually raise manufacturer revenue but often not retailer revenue or margins. Who gains depends on brand and category characteristics.
course_use: Background for trade promotions and manufacturer-retailer negotiations. WU-Lizenz prüfen (INFORMS).

title: How to Fight a Price War
author_source: Rao, A. R.; Bergen, M. E.; Davis, S., Harvard Business Review 78(2), 2000, article
note: Practitioner framework for preventing, avoiding and, if necessary, fighting price wars: diagnose the causes, use non-price responses and retaliate selectively. Many examples.
course_use: Core practitioner reading on price wars; combine with Van Heerde et al. (2008) as the empirical case. Paid HBR, WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Winners and Losers in a Major Price War
author_source: Van Heerde, H. J.; Gijsbrechts, E.; Pauwels, K., Journal of Marketing Research 45(5), 499-518, 2008, article
note: Analysis of the 2003 Dutch supermarket price war started by Albert Heijn: the initiator did not gain as expected, and effects on store traffic and share differed across chains. Shows the real costs of price wars.
course_use: Case-like reading on price wars; draw parallels to Austrian grocery discounting (Hofer, Spar, Billa). WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Supermarket Pricing Strategies
author_source: Ellickson, P. B.; Misra, S., Marketing Science 27(5), 811-828, 2008, article
note: US supermarket data showing that EDLP and Hi-Lo choices are strategic complements in local markets (stores tend to match rivals' formats) and depend on store and consumer demographics.
course_use: Reading for EDLP vs. Hi-Lo; students classify Austrian retailers by price format. WU-Lizenz prüfen (INFORMS).

title: Shopping Behavior and Consumer Preference for Store Price Format: Why "Large Basket" Shoppers Prefer EDLP
author_source: Bell, D. R.; Lattin, J. M., Marketing Science 17(1), 66-88, 1998, article
note: Shows that large-basket shoppers prefer EDLP stores and small-basket shoppers prefer Hi-Lo stores, which explains why both formats coexist.
course_use: Classic pair with Ellickson and Misra. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Frontiers: Shrinkflation Aversion: When and Why Product Size Decreases Are Seen as More Unfair than Equivalent Price Increases
author_source: Evangelidis, I., Marketing Science 43(2), 280-288, 2024, article
note: Experiments showing that consumers who notice package downsizing judge it more unfair than an equivalent price increase, because it is seen as deceptive. Key for the inflation-era pricing discussion.
course_use: Core reading on shrinkflation; combine with Janssen and Kasinger to contrast perceptions with actual behaviour. WU-Lizenz prüfen (INFORMS).

title: Shrinkflation and Consumer Demand
author_source: Janssen, A.; Kasinger, J., Marketing Science 45(1), 142-158, 2026, article
note: Decade-long US grocery scanner data: shrinkflation is widespread and consumers barely adjust demand despite higher per-unit prices, so downsizing works commercially because it is rarely noticed. An SSRN version is available (10.2139/ssrn.4783491).
course_use: Debate: fairness perceptions (Evangelidis) vs. actual demand response; link to the EU/Austrian labelling debate. WU-Lizenz prüfen; SSRN version free.

title: Consumers' preference for downsizing over package price increases
author_source: Kim, I., Journal of Economics & Management Strategy, 2023, article
note: Natural experiment from South Korean milk producers reacting to 2018 cost increases: for the same unit-price rise, consumers strongly preferred downsizing to package price increases, and this preference did not fade over time.
course_use: Evidence for why firms choose shrinkflation; pair with the fairness readings. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Wiley).

title: Consumer Response to Package Downsizing: Evidence from the Chicago Ice Cream Market
author_source: Çakır, M.; Balagtas, J. V., Journal of Retailing 90(1), 1-12, 2014, article
note: Classic from before the recent inflation wave, estimating demand responses to ice cream package downsizing: consumers react far less to size reductions than to equivalent price increases.
course_use: Background classic for the shrinkflation block. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Elsevier).

title: How B2B Firms Can Price with Confidence as Inflation Rises
author_source: Mehta, N.; Burton, M., Harvard Business Review (HBR.org), November 2021, article (republished by Bain & Company)
note: Practitioner article by Bain consultants arguing that incremental, across-the-board price increases are not enough during inflation and that firms should hedge against prolonged inflation; it proposes five strategies for managing necessary increases. The link is Bain's republished copy; the original HBR.org URL could not be confirmed.
course_use: Short pre-reading for the inflation-era pricing discussion; pair with Homburg et al. (2005) and Zbaracki et al. (2004). Free (Bain copy).

title: Dynamics of Price Elasticity and Brand Life Cycles: An Empirical Study
author_source: Simon, H., Journal of Marketing Research 16(4), 439-452, 1979, article
note: Hermann Simon's early empirical study showing that price elasticities change systematically over the brand life cycle. Foundation for pricing strategy across the life cycle.
course_use: Historical anchor for German pricing research (Simon is co-founder of Simon-Kucher); short discussion of life-cycle pricing. WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Price fairness
author_source: Diller, H., Journal of Product & Brand Management 17(5), 353-355, 2008, article
note: Short editorial by Hermann Diller (Erlangen-Nürnberg) introducing a journal section on price fairness and outlining it as a multidimensional construct. Content summarised from the title and the author's known work; skim before assigning.
course_use: Very short entry point to German-school thinking on price fairness; use as an introduction to the fairness readings. WU-Lizenz prüfen (Emerald).
